sections.b: John 11 tells the longest miracle story in the Gospels. Lazarus falls sick; Jesus waits two days and arrives when Lazarus has been four days in the tomb. He tells Martha, "I am the resurrection and the life" (John 11:25), weeps at the grave, and calls Lazarus out by name. John makes it the last and greatest of Jesus' signs, and the reason the council decides Jesus must die (John 11:45–53). The chief priests then plan to kill Lazarus too, because many believe on his account (John 12:9–11).

The two sisters act alike in Luke and John. Martha is active: she serves (Luke 10:40; John 12:2), goes out to meet Jesus, and makes a full confession of faith, "you are the Messiah, the Son of God" (John 11:27). Mary sits at Jesus' feet to listen (Luke 10:39), falls at his feet in grief (John 11:32), and anoints his feet with nard (John 12:3). Western tradition from Gregory the Great (591) merged Mary of Bethany with the sinful woman of Luke 7 and with Mary Magdalene; the Eastern churches and most modern scholars keep the three apart.

Matthew, Mark and Luke do not mention Lazarus. Some think they focused on Galilee; Richard Bauckham argues for "protective anonymity," since Lazarus was in danger in Jerusalem (John 12:10); many critical scholars think John's tradition developed the story, perhaps in dialogue with Luke 16:19–31, where a Lazarus who rises would not convince the unbelieving. Some have suggested that Lazarus was the Beloved Disciple, since he alone is named as one Jesus loved (John 11:3, 5, 36), but most scholars find this unlikely.

common: Jesus raised his friend Lazarus after four days in the tomb, the greatest of his signs in John.
uncommon: Lazarus was the Beloved Disciple who wrote, or stands behind, the Gospel of John.

sections.b: In John, the festival crowd hears that Jesus is coming and goes out with palm branches, crying "Hosanna! Blessed is the one who comes in the Lord's name, yes, the King of Israel!" (John 12:13). Only then does Jesus find a young donkey and sit on it, fulfilling a short form of Zechariah 9:9. Only John mentions palms, symbols of national victory since the Maccabees (1 Maccabees 13:51), and only John says the crowd came because of the raising of Lazarus (John 12:17–18). Many read the donkey as Jesus' answer to the crowd's hope for a warrior king. John admits the disciples understood it only after Jesus was glorified (John 12:16).

common: The crowds who shouted "Hosanna" were the same people who shouted "Crucify him" a few days later (a popular idea; the Gospels never say so, and the festival crowd and the crowd at Pilate's court may well have been different people).
uncommon: In John, Jesus deliberately mounted the donkey after the crowd's royal welcome, to correct their idea of what kind of king he was.

sections.h: "I am the resurrection and the life"
sections.b: Martha voices the Jewish hope of a resurrection "on the last day" (John 11:24). Jesus answers that he himself is the resurrection and the life: those who believe in him will live even if they die, and those who live and believe will never die (John 11:25–26). John keeps both a present gift of life and a future bodily rising (John 5:24–29; 6:40). The raising of Lazarus is a sign of both, though Lazarus returns to ordinary life and will die again, unlike Jesus, who leaves his grave clothes behind (John 11:44; 20:5–7). Jesus' calling death "sleep" (John 11:11–14) has been read by some churches as teaching that the dead are unconscious until the resurrection.

claude.title: Two tombs
claude.body: John seems to tell the tomb of Lazarus and the tomb of Jesus as a matched pair: a cave and a stone, a weeping Mary, a question of where the body is, and grave clothes, worn by Lazarus as he comes out but left behind by Jesus. The contrast marks the difference between being brought back to this life and rising to a life that does not end.

sections.b: Six days before Passover, Mary of Bethany pours a pound of costly nard on Jesus' feet and wipes them with her hair (John 12:3). Mark and Matthew tell of an unnamed woman anointing his head in Bethany (Mark 14:3–9; Matthew 26:6–13); Luke tells of a sinful woman anointing his feet in Galilee (Luke 7:36–50). Kings were anointed on the head, but in John the anointing is at the feet and, by Jesus' own word, for his burial (John 12:7). The anointed one, the Messiah, is anointed for death.

Lazarus is buried the day he dies in a rock-cut cave closed by a stone, wrapped in strips of cloth with a cloth over his face (John 11:38, 44). Friends come from Jerusalem to comfort the sisters during the seven days of mourning, and the mourners wail at the tomb (John 11:19, 31). Martha's "he already stinks" shows that no embalming was done (John 11:39). Mary's anointing of Jesus is, he says, for the day of his burial (John 12:7).

In John, Jesus' death is his glorification. Lazarus' sickness is "for God's glory" (John 11:4), and when the Greeks come Jesus says, "The hour is here when the Son of Man will be glorified" (John 12:23). The voice from heaven promises to glorify the Father's name again (John 12:28). John says Isaiah "had seen his glory" (John 12:41), linking the throne vision of Isaiah 6 with Christ, and he contrasts that glory with "the glory people give," which many leaders preferred (John 12:43).
sections.refs: John 11:4; John 11:40; John 12:23; John 12:28; John 12:41–43; Isaiah 6:1–5; Isaiah 52:13

sections.b: The crowd that meets Jesus outside Jerusalem shouts the last psalm of the Hallel: "Hosanna!" from Psalm 118:25 (Hebrew "save, please!") and "Blessed is the one who comes in the Lord's name" from Psalm 118:26, adding "the King of Israel" (John 12:13). Pilgrims sang these psalms at Passover, so the words were on everyone's lips that week.

Martha confesses Jesus as "the Messiah, the Son of God, the one coming into the world" (John 11:27), the very words of the Gospel's purpose (John 20:31). But when Jesus speaks of being lifted up, the crowd objects that the Law says "the Messiah remains forever" (John 12:34), probably thinking of Psalm 89:36, where David's offspring last forever. A dying Messiah did not fit their expectation.

At the close of Jesus' public ministry John explains the unbelief of many by Isaiah 6:10, in a form where God himself blinds eyes and hardens hearts (John 12:39–40). Yet he adds at once that many leaders did believe but kept quiet (John 12:42), and that those who reject Jesus' word are judged by it (John 12:48). Paul uses similar texts and insists the hardening is partial and temporary (Romans 11:7–10, 25–26).

Jesus says that once lifted up he will draw everyone to himself (John 12:32), the same verb as "unless the Father ... draws him" (John 6:44). Reformed readers take "everyone" as all kinds of people, Jews and Greeks, effectually drawn; Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Methodist and many Baptist readers take it as a drawing offered to every person that can be resisted. Some early manuscripts and the Latin Vulgate read "all things."

sections.h: The ruler of this world thrown out
sections.b: John calls the devil "this world's ruler" (John 12:31; 14:30; 16:11). As the hour of the cross comes, Jesus says he "will be thrown out" (John 12:31): the cross, which looks like the world's verdict on Jesus, is the world's judgment and Satan's defeat. Compare Revelation 12:9–10, where the dragon is thrown down.

Jesus' third saying about being "lifted up" (John 3:14; 8:28; 12:32) is explained by the narrator: it pointed to the kind of death he would die (John 12:33), raised on a cross as the bronze snake was raised on a pole (Numbers 21:9). The same verb also means "exalted," as in the Greek of Isaiah 52:13, where the servant is lifted up and glorified.

John quotes Isaiah 53:1 in its Greek form to explain unbelief (John 12:38), and his language of Jesus being "lifted up" and "glorified" (John 12:23, 32) matches the Greek of Isaiah 52:13, the opening of the servant song. Caiaphas' unwitting prophecy that one man should die for the people (John 11:50–52) also echoes the servant who bears the sins of many.
sections.refs: John 12:38; Isaiah 53:1; Isaiah 52:13; John 12:23; John 12:32; John 11:50–52

sections.b: These chapters show the range of the word. "The Jews" who wanted to stone Jesus are the Jerusalem opponents (John 11:8); "the Jews" who come to comfort Martha and Mary, weep with them and see Jesus' love are friends (John 11:19, 31, 36); many of them believe (John 11:45; 12:11). The plot is the work of "the chief priests and the Pharisees" in council (John 11:47–53; 12:10). Even "many among the rulers" believe but fear being thrown out of the synagogue (John 12:42), a word whose background is debated.

Joseph Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36 under Roman governors (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 18.35, 95), and an ossuary inscribed "Joseph son of Caiaphas" was found in Jerusalem in 1990. In John he advises the council that one man should die for the people, and John calls it a prophecy given through his office (John 11:49–52). The chief priests lead the plot against Jesus and against Lazarus (John 11:47, 57; 12:10).

John names three Passovers (John 2:13; 6:4; 11:55), the basis for speaking of a three-year ministry. Before the last one, pilgrims come up early to purify themselves (John 11:55), Mary anoints Jesus six days before the feast (John 12:1), and the entry follows the next day.

sections.h: Greeks who want to see Jesus
sections.b: Some Greeks, Gentiles who had come up to worship at Passover, ask Philip, "Sir, we want to see Jesus" (John 12:21). Their coming signals that Jesus' hour has come and points to the many from the nations whom he will draw when lifted up (John 12:23, 32; compare John 10:16; 11:52).

John says Caiaphas did not speak "from himself": as high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation and gather God's scattered children (John 11:51–52). Like Balaam (Numbers 23–24), he spoke truer than he meant.

When Judas objects that the nard could have been sold for the poor, Jesus answers with Deuteronomy 15:11 (John 12:8). In Deuteronomy the lasting presence of the poor is the reason to keep giving; Jesus' point is that his own time is short. The saying has often been misused to excuse indifference to poverty.

The fifth "I am" saying with a picture is spoken to Martha at her brother's death: "I am the resurrection and the life" (John 11:25). It moves the hope of the last day into the person of Jesus, present in front of her.

sections.h: The King of Israel on a donkey
sections.b: The crowd hails Jesus as "the King of Israel" with palms of victory (John 12:13), and he answers by sitting on a young donkey, as Zechariah's humble king does (John 12:14–15; Zechariah 9:9–10).

sections.h: Jesus speaks only the Father's words
sections.b: Jesus' closing public words echo Deuteronomy 18:18–19: he does not speak from himself; the Father who sent him commanded what he should say, and those who reject his words will be judged by them (John 12:48–50).

Jesus urges the crowd to walk while they have the light and believe in the light so as to become "sons of light" (John 12:35–36), language shared with the Dead Sea Scrolls' contrast of sons of light and sons of darkness.

Only John names Judas as the disciple who objected to Mary's anointing, saying the nard could have been sold for three hundred denarii for the poor, and only John says he was a thief who kept the common purse and took from it (John 12:4–6). Mark and Matthew give the objection to "some" or "the disciples" and place Judas' deal with the chief priests right after the anointing (Mark 14:4–11; Matthew 26:8–16).

John 11:47–53 tells how the chief priests and Pharisees in council decided Jesus must die, for fear that Rome would destroy "our place and our nation." The text describes a decision of a few leaders under Roman rule; the same chapter shows many Jews mourning with Martha and Mary and believing in Jesus (John 11:19, 45). Later Christian use of such scenes to blame all Jews for Jesus' death was rejected by the Second Vatican Council (Nostra Aetate 4) and most churches.
